newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba says German economy back on track for growth.
newsitem.headline: Buba says German economy back on track for growth.

text.p: Germany is not out of the woods yet but the economy is back on track for growth after emerging from a spate of weakness in late 1996, the Bundesbank said in its June monthly report on Wednesday.
"In the first months of 1997, the German economy has overcome the doldrums into which it fell in autumn of last year and is now back on track from growth," the report said.
The Bundesbank said strong impulses from the export side continued to be the dominant force, while domestic demand has so far not yet picked up convincingly despite a series of favorable conditions.
The Bundesbank also said the mark has fallen to a level that roughly reflects underlying economic fundamentals.

The German central bank said heavy industry and the services sector had developed favourably so far in 1997, while the construction industry had suffered serious drops in output, particularly in the new eastern states.
The German central bank however noted that structural problems -- such as an inflexible labour market -- were holding the country back from cyclical growth.
"The German economy is still confronted with many structural problems which tend to brake the cyclical upward trend," the report said.
One side-effect of the slow growth has been continued high unemployment -- a problem the Bundesbank was not optimstic could soon be overcome.

"The jobs market situation shows a gloomy picture overall at the start of 1997," the Bundesbank said, explaining the average number of those in work in the first quarter, after seasonal adjustments, was down 0.7 percent from autumn 1996 at 34.05 million.
The slow growth was helping to reduce the threat of inflation and prospects for a German interest rate hike.
"At the moment, inflationary impulses are not recognisable either from the demand side or from cost pressures," the central bank said.
Commenting on its "steady hand" monetary policy, the Bundesbank said it would make sure to safeguard price stability over the long-term.
"All available indicators speak for further expansion in the good export economy, even if growth in the future does not remain in double-digit figures," the report said.

Trade with European Union nations remained important since they account for three-fifths of German exports. But the report noted a short-term drop in exports to the United States, other European nations, southeast Asia and eastern Europe.
But the report noted the stronger dollar led to higher import prices in the first quarter, rising 3.5 percent over the 1996 fourth quarter and nine percent over the first quarter.
The central bank also said Germany's federal, regional and municipal budget deficits are likely to exceed Bonn's plans for 1997 but that the social insurance system should swing to a surplus.
It added that tax revenues had partly been squeezed by special factors in the opening months of 1997 and were likely to become less unfavourable during the rest of the year.
